'''Kumomi Sengen Shrine''' (雲見浅間神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} located on {{ill|Mount Eboshi (Matsuzaki, Shizuoka)|ja|烏帽子山 (松崎町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Eboshi (Matsuzaki, Shizuoka)|1=Mount Eboshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q47461946}}, with an elevation of 162 meters, in {{ill|Kumomi Onsen|ja|雲見温泉|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumomi Onsen|1=Kumomi Onsen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11660083}}, {{ill|Matsuzaki, Shizuoka|en|Matsuzaki, Shizuoka|qid=Q1204017|lt=Matsuzaki, Shizuoka|1=Matsuzaki, Shizuoka}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|qid=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture|1=Shizuoka Prefecture}}, Japan. It is also known as '''Kumomi Shrine''' (雲見神社) or '''Ontake Sengen Shrine''' (御嶽浅間宮). It is one of the rare [[Sengen shrine|Asama Shrines]] dedicated solely to {{ill|Iwanaga-hime|lt=Iwanaga-hime no Mikoto|ja|磐長姫尊|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iwanaga-hime|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.

== Overview ==
Mount Eboshi, also called Ontake (御嶽山) or Kumomi-ga-take (雲見ヶ嶽), is a stand-alone {{ill|Tuff|en|Tuff|qid=Q484924|lt=Tuff|1=Tuff}} rock formation located at the westernmost coast of the Izu Peninsula. The shrine's main hall is located just below the summit, while the worship hall and the middle shrine (Nakanomiya) are on the mountain's slopes. Historically, the shrine was off-limits to women, who were only allowed to worship at the middle shrine.

From the base at {{ill|Japan National Route 136|en|Japan National Route 136|qid=Q11421406|lt=National Route 136 (Japan)|1=Japan National Route 136}}, the shrine is accessible by a steep 25-minute climb, passing two worship halls before reaching the main shrine. The 428-step stone stairway is extremely steep and includes sections with unstable footing. Due to strong winds near the summit, visitors require sturdy footwear, and light clothing such as high heels is strongly discouraged.

== History ==
The founding date and origins are unknown. It is traditionally identified with "Ishito no Myojin," listed as "Conferred Fourth Rank, Upper Grade" in the ''Izu Province Shrine Ranking Book,'' and believed to correspond to "Iwanohime no Mikoto Shrine" in the ''Engishiki Jinmyōchō,'' although conclusive evidence is lacking.

According to the ''Zushu Shiko,'' the name "Ishito no Myojin" derives from a stone gate called "Asama-mon" in the sea, likely referring to the '''Senganmon''' rock formation about 800 meters south of Mount Eboshi. Shrine lore recounts that the main hall was swept into the sea by a typhoon and rebuilt in {{ill|1657|en|1657|qid=Q6987|lt=1657|1=1657}} (Meireki 3).

The shrine was a center for [[Shinbutsu-shūgō]] (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism) and visited by ascetics until the [[Meiji Restoration]] when it was designated as a [[Gōsha]] following the separation of Shinto and Buddhism. After the abolition of the shrine Ranking system post-{{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|qid=Q184425|lt=Pacific War|1=Pacific War}}, local residents have maintained the shrine.

== Legends ==
{{ill|Iwanaga-hime|lt=Iwanaga-hime no Mikoto|ja|磐長姫尊|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iwanaga-hime|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the enshrined deity, is the sister of {{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|ja|木花咲耶姫命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Konohanasakuya-hime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to QID FIXED|qid=Q1781862}}, the deity of {{ill|Mount Fuji|en|Mount Fuji|qid=Q39231|lt=Mount Fuji|1=Mount Fuji}} and the [[Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha|Fujisan Hongŭ Sengen Taisha]], and daughter of {{ill|Ōyamatsumi|ja|大山祗命|1=Ōyamatsumi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyamatsumi|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyamatsumi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to QID FIXED|qid=Q386563}}.

In mythology, Iwanaga-hime was considered unattractive but promised longevity like a rock to her offspring, while her beautiful sister Konohanasakuya-hime’s children were destined for short lives like flowers. The heavenly grandson {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|lt=Ninigi-no-Mikoto|lt=Ninigi|ja|瓊瓊杵命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninigi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ニニギ}} rejected Iwanaga-hime, causing her to retreat to Kumomi, leading to enmity between the once-close sisters.

According to {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|en|Motoori Norinaga|qid=Q384647|lt=Motoori Norinaga|1=Motoori Norinaga}}'s ''Kojikiden,'' the jealous Iwanaga-hime fled to Kumomi, where she was enshrined on a small rocky mountain, while her kind sister stretched tall to look for her, becoming the towering Mount Fuji. Local legends say that when Mount Eboshi is clear, Mount Fuji is shrouded in clouds, and vice versa. Praising Mount Fuji from Mount Eboshi is said to invite misfortune, and "Fuji" was once taboo in local speech.
